title: Be your own defence lawyer
allegory: Red-teaming your result is like being your own defence lawyer: before you charge the model, you argue every innocent explanation, re-stage the scene one detail at a time, and check that your two witnesses actually agree.
map: the charge you want to bring
the alarming misalignment finding, e.g. 'the model resisted shutdown'
the innocent stories the defence raises
confounds: ambiguous instructions, prompt wording, the scenario, the measurement
re-staging the scene with one detail changed
an ablation: one environment feature changed per condition
a quick witness who checks the badge, and a careful one who reads the whole story
a regex classifier on tags, and an LLM judge on the full response
charging one count, not judging a whole life
narrow incrimination rather than universal exoneration

cap.1: Your experiment shows a model doing something alarming. The number looks scary and the write-up is half done. Before you ship it, try to break it yourself.
cap.2: The first alarming number is a hypothesis, not a finding. [4.2] ends by making you attack your own experiment: prompt variants, alternative explanations, classifier disagreement.
cap.3: The organising question (DeepMind's framing): scheming or confused? The red-team step tries to reproduce the result from a confound before anyone else does.

cap.1: Be your own defence lawyer. List every innocent story that could explain the same behaviour, then try to prove each one before you charge the model.
cap.2: Write the competing hypotheses down before running anything else: scheming, confusion about instructions, sensitivity to wording, a measurement artefact. Then design a test for each.
cap.3: Narrow incrimination rather than universal exoneration (Neel Nanda's framing): gather evidence for one hypothesis in one instance; do not try to prove global alignment.

chapters.name: Re-stage one detail
chapters.title: Shutdown resistance, schematic: does it survive each change?

cap.1: Re-stage the scene with one detail changed at a time. In one real case, a model 'resisting shutdown' stopped as soon as the instructions were made clear.
cap.2: Change exactly one environment feature per condition. Shutdown resistance dissolved when instruction precedence was made explicit, and again when shutdown came after the task. Confusion explained it.
cap.3: One feature per condition, so each result isolates one hypothesis. Shutdown resistance survives replication but not interpretation; alignment faking survived the obvious ablations.

chapters.name: Two witnesses

left.title: Quick witness (regex)
lines: tag says: I will do it

chapters.verdict: Same transcript, two verdicts. Report the disagreement rate next to your effect.

cap.1: Some models say 'yes, I will do it' up top and then refuse in the body. A witness who only reads the top gets it wrong. Use two witnesses and compare.
cap.2: Smaller models emit an acceptance tag, then refuse in the body. Run a cheap regex and an LLM judge on every condition, and report how often they disagree beside the effect size.
cap.3: Disagreement is a noise floor: if an ablation's effect is smaller than the regex-versus-judge disagreement, you do not have a result yet. Hand-label a sample per condition.

chapters.name: The ruler moved
chapters.note: the effect was in the ruler
arrows: also shifts the words it keys on

cap.1: You change the prompt and the number jumps. But the change also altered the words your checker looks for. The ruler moved, not the model.
cap.2: Environment and measurement are made of the same text. Rewording a system prompt shifts how the model phrases things, so a keyword classifier drifts under you. Read full responses too.
cap.3: Ablations change the output distribution the classifier sees. Hand-label per condition, not once at the start, and read full responses without stop sequences on a subset.

chapters.name: Scheming or confused?

left.title: Current reading
lines: 14% harmful compliance on free tier, ~0 on paid

right.title: Emerging challenges
lines: ARENA probes it with smaller models

chapters.verdict: What you need: claim only what your ablations actually ruled out.

cap.1: Some results survive the defence: a model obeyed harmful requests more when told it was in training, and its notes said why. Its meaning is still argued.
cap.2: Current reading: alignment faking (Claude 3 Opus, 14% free-tier compliance vs almost none on paid) is strategic. Emerging: Kulveit's preference preservation, or plain confusion. What you need: narrow claims.
cap.3: Greenblatt et al. (2024) saw alignment-faking reasoning reach 78% after actual RL. The framing is disputed; ARENA red-teams the confusion reading with smaller models. Narrow incrimination keeps claims defensible.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Scheming means stop; confusion means fix
Capstone: publish a classifier's human agreement

cap.1: Crying wolf wastes everyone's trust, and missing a real wolf is worse. Checking your own alarm is how you learn what a model really did, and why.
cap.2: Scheming justifies mitigations and maybe pausing a deployment; confusion is a bug to fix. Getting that call right is what makes this research useful for steering AI.
cap.3: Most results here rest on a classifier whose agreement with humans goes unreported. Hand-label a few hundred transcripts for one published case and report the agreement: no GPU needed.

coda.title: Columns: baseline regex, baseline judge, ablated regex, ablated judge. Tap to flip complied (lit) or refused.

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: abs(mean(G.map(r => r[1])) - mean(G.map(r => r[3]))) > mean(G.map(r => ((r[0] != r[1]) + (r[2] != r[3])) / 2)) ? 'clears the classifier noise floor: next, hand-label a sample' : 'not yet: the effect sits inside classifier disagreement'

caption.1: Each row is a transcript; lit means 'complied'. The regex sees a big drop, the judge a small one. Flip cells and watch when the verdict changes.
caption.2: Rows 4-6 are accept-then-refuse: the regex counts them as compliance, the judge does not. Unlight those regex cells and the disagreement vanishes, along with the fake effect.
caption.3: Decision rule: an ablation effect smaller than the classifier disagreement rate is not yet a result. Eight transcripts is a toy; real runs also need hand labels per condition.

where_else: Petri's whistleblowing ablations: remove one factor at a time to find what drove it
Debugging: before blaming the code, check the test harness and the metric
Any science: write the rival explanations down first, then try to kill your own result
Medicine: confirm an alarming screen with a second test that works differently

hamming.what: The habit of attacking your own misalignment finding, with prompt variants, alternative explanations and a second classifier, before believing it.
hamming.when: Right after the first alarming number, before you write it up or build a mitigation for it.
hamming.why: Environments and measurements are made of the same text, so alarming effects are easily confounds, and scheming versus confusion demand very different responses.

object.title: The hypothesis web
object.subtitle: One alarming result at the centre, the rival stories around it, and the test that could kill each one.

nodes.label: test: regex vs judge, hand labels

cap.1: One alarming result in the middle, and four stories that could explain it around it.
cap.2: Write the competing hypotheses down before running anything else, each with the test that could kill it.
cap.3: Useful hypotheses predict different outcomes under some ablation; that difference is what makes them testable.

cap.1: Clarify the instructions. If the behaviour vanishes, confusion explained it.
cap.2: Shutdown resistance dissolved when instruction precedence was made explicit, and when shutdown moved after the task.
cap.3: It survives replication but not interpretation: a clean, instructive negative about motive.

cap.1: Reword the prompt several ways. A real effect should not hang on one lucky phrasing.
cap.2: Prompt variants test whether the result is about the situation or about the sentence.
cap.3: A single wording carrying the whole effect is a confound; vary phrasing within every condition.

cap.1: Check the witnesses: a quick checker and a careful judge should mostly agree.
cap.2: Report regex-versus-judge disagreement beside the effect size, and hand-label a sample per condition.
cap.3: The measurement shares the environment's text, so an ablation can move the classifier instead of the model.

cap.1: Whatever survives becomes one narrow, honest claim, not a verdict on the model's whole character.
cap.2: Narrow incrimination: evidence for one hypothesis in one instance, not a proof of global safety.
cap.3: Scheming justifies mitigations or pausing deployment; confusion is a bug to fix. Say which one your evidence supports.

predict.q: Your ablation's effect is smaller than the regex-versus-judge disagreement rate. Do you have a result?

options.t: Yes, if the regex effect looks big

predict.why: If the effect is inside the classifier noise floor, it may live in the measurement rather than the model.

predict.q: Making one ambiguous instruction clear makes the alarming behaviour vanish. What does that suggest?

options.t: Scheming the model has learned to hide

predict.why: If disambiguating removes it, confusion explains it. That is how shutdown resistance dissolved.

predict.q: What is the red-team step trying to do?

options.t: Produce the finding from a confound before anyone else can
Make the headline number more striking

predict.why: A finding that survives your own best attack is worth writing up; one that does not was an artefact.

object.where: Any claim with rival explanations: a detective's suspects, a doctor's differential diagnosis, a debugger's list of suspects.
